query: Consider the following context: High-entropy alloy (HEA) multilayers represent a promising class of advanced coating materials due to their superior mechanical properties, corrosion resistance, and irradiation tolerance. However, the specific role of interface coherency on the creep behavior of HEA multilayers remains unclear. In that context, which material can be used for transition between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep mechanisms, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a tunable NiAl interlayer into HEA multilayers will enable a controlled transition from diffusion‐mediated to dislocation‐mediated creep by establishing highly coherent interfaces and providing intermediate atomic diffusivity.
generation.material_initial_state: Multilayer coatings composed of HEA layers with designed coherent interfaces.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a NiAl interlayer with controlled thickness and adjusted composition between HEA layers.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures under creep conditions where both diffusion and dislocation creep mechanisms are active.
generation.structural_mediator: Highly coherent interfaces between the NiAl interlayer and adjacent HEA layers.
generation.mechanism: The NiAl interlayer, thanks to its ability to form coherent interfaces with many FCC HEA matrices and its intermediate diffusivity, modulates the balance between atomic diffusion and dislocation mobility. This creates a transitional region where the creep mechanism gradually shifts from being dominated by atomic diffusion at lower stresses/temperatures to being governed by dislocation movements at higher stresses/temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The creep behavior of the multilayer will show a measurable shift: lower applied stresses or temperatures will favor diffusion creep, while higher stresses or temperatures will trigger dislocation-mediated creep. This transition will be more controlled and occur at intermediate conditions compared to HEA multilayers without a NiAl interlayer.
generation.baseline: HEA multilayers without the NiAl interlayer, where the transition between creep mechanisms is less defined and not intentionally regulated.
generation.boundary: The effect depends on the maintenance of interface coherency and precise interlayer control; excessive thickness or compositional deviations may degrade coherency, limiting the transitional effect.
generation.uncertainty: The exact stress and temperature thresholds for the mechanism switch remain uncertain and will require detailed experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA multilayer samples – one with a NiAl interlayer (with tunable thickness and composition) and one without. Subject both sets to a series of high-temperature creep tests while systematically varying the stress and temperature. Use TEM and XRD to assess interface coherency, and apply dislocation analysis techniques to identify the dominant creep mechanism in each regime.
measurements: Creep strain rate and yield stress under varying conditions
Dislocation density and activity (via microscopic analysis)
Atomic diffusivity estimates from the interlayer region
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of the NiAl interlayer does not result in a distinct and reproducible shift from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep—i.e., if the creep behavior of samples with the NiAl interlayer is statistically indistinguishable from that of the samples without it—then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Various industrial and advanced functional applications require materials with high strength and ductility. Unfortunately, conventional processing strategies usually attain high material strength at the expense of deteriorated ductility [1] – [3] , whilst developing structures with substantial improvement of both strength and ductility is highly challenging. Recent successes in synthesizing superhard materials [4] – [6] have made the high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment [7] , [8] promising to achieve extreme properties in materials. The combination of pressure and temperature offers the great prospect for altering the microstructure of structural materials that would permit overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off. Given the vast space of control parameters involved in the HPHT treatment and the often complex microstructural evolution under extreme pressures and temperatures [9] , [10] , it remains difficult to predict and interpret the mechanical behaviors of HPHT-treated structural materials, especially the abnormal kinetics and thermodynamics of non-equilibrium interfaces induced by the HPHT treatment [11] , [12] .

decision.trend: Early studies on HEAs focused on deciphering bulk creep mechanisms – identifying diffusion-mediated creep at lower stresses/temperatures and dislocation-mediated creep at higher driving forces – but the role of interfaces was not isolated. More recent work, particularly that on HPHT-treated HEAs showing near‐zero mismatch factors between coexisting phases (PMC11087546), has highlighted that highly coherent interfaces can strongly influence the activation of dislocation‐driven deformation. While the traditional studies (e.g. PMC7512559) characterized creep behavior in monolithic HEAs, the emerging trend is toward engineering interfaces (as in multilayer coatings) to deliberately mediate the transition between mechanisms. However, it remains unsolved how to select and optimize an interlayer material that provides an intermediate response – balancing a moderate diffusion rate and dislocation mobility – to tune the creep mechanism.
decision.unsolved: How to design a transition interlayer material in HEA multilayers that simultaneously maintains high interface coherency and offers a controlled balance between atomic diffusivity and dislocation mobility to switch from diffusion-mediated to dislocation-mediated creep remains unclear.
decision.lever: Introduce a NiAl interlayer with tunable thickness and composition to precisely control the lattice mismatch with adjacent HEA layers
decision.why: NiAl is known to form highly coherent interfaces with many FCC HEA matrices and possesses intermediate diffusivity. This makes it a promising candidate to bridge the gap between diffusion and dislocation creep mechanisms, which directly follows the trend of tailoring interface properties in HEA multilayers to pinpoint and control the creep transition.
